student_passage:
Cooling Without Winter

[1] Before mechanical refrigeration, people cooled food and drink with evaporation or ice collected during cold weather. [2] Stored ice could last into summer, but its supply depended on winter temperatures, insulation, and transportation. [3] During the nineteenth century, inventors began developing machines that could produce cooling without waiting for a pond to freeze.[1]

The commercial ice trade had already turned frozen water into a widely distributed product. Workers captured[2] blocks from lakes and rivers, then cut moved and packed[3] them into insulated buildings. Sawdust and other loose materials filled wall cavities, slowing the movement of heat into an icehouse.[4] Ice could then travel by wagon or ship to homes, markets, and businesses.

Natural ice was useful, but its size diminished as it absorbed heat. Warm winters could also reduce the supply. Nevertheless,[5] breweries, food processors, and other industries wanted a controllable source of cooling throughout the year. Mechanical systems offered a different approach: instead of delivering a cold object, they repeatedly moved heat away from a chosen space.

A set of sealed pipes and components carry[6] a working fluid called a refrigerant through a cycle. Inside the cooled area, the refrigerant evaporates and gobbles[7] heat. A compressor then raises the pressure of the vapor, outside the cooled area, the vapor releases heat and condenses into a liquid.[8] The liquid returns to the interior portion of the system, where the cycle begins again.

[A] Early refrigeration machines were large and required skilled attention. [B] Factories and warehouses adopted the technology before compact household units became common.[9] [C] Improved motors, controls, insulation, and manufacturing gradually made smaller systems more practical. [D] Refrigerators eventually allowed households to maintain a steady cold space without arranging repeated deliveries of harvested ice.

Mechanical refrigeration did more than imitate an icebox. By circulating a refrigerant, the system made cooling continuous, adjustable, and less dependent on local weather. The central achievement was not the creation of cold as a substance, but the controlled transfer of heat from one place to another.[10]
